L	India’s cities are expanding at a pace that outstrips both imagination and infrastructure. Glass
towers rise where wetlands once filtered rainwater; expressways carve through once-cohesive
neighbourhoods in the name of “connectivity.” Yet beneath the spectacle of cranes and concrete
lies a quieter crisis — the systematic erosion of urban resilience.
Policymakers often invoke the rhetoric of “world-class cities,” borrowing architectural
templates from Singapore or Shanghai, but seldom pausing to interrogate whether such
blueprints align with local ecological and social realities. Urban development, when reduced to
an aesthetic contest of skylines, becomes a mirage: shimmering in promise, but fragile in
substance.
The consequences are neither abstract nor distant. Flooded basements during monsoon
months, heat islands that trap entire populations in sweltering discomfort, and informal
settlements pushed to city peripheries reveal the fault lines in planning. The paradox is
striking — cities are engines of growth, yet they are also sites of deepening inequality.
A sustainable urban future demands more than cosmetic innovation. It requires participatory
governance, ecological literacy, and the humility to recognise that development is not
synonymous with displacement. Until urban policy shifts from spectacle to substance, India’s
cities will continue to expand upward while hollowing inward.
Source: The Hindu, Editorial Section, Title: The Mirage of Instant Urbanism

I.	In an age where notifications punctuate silence with mechanical urgency, attention has
become both commodity and casualty. Digital platforms compete not merely for users, but for
minutes, clicks, and fragments of cognitive presence. What was once idle browsing has evolved
into an engineered ecosystem of persuasion, calibrated through algorithms that anticipate
desire before it is consciously formed.
The architecture of the digital marketplace thrives on engagement metrics. Infinite scroll,
autoplay features, and algorithmic recommendations are not neutral conveniences; they are
deliberate design choices rooted in behavioural psychology. The objective is simple: prolong
interaction. The cost, however, is diffuse yet profound — diminished concentration, fractured
discourse, and a public sphere increasingly shaped by outrage rather than deliberation.
Defenders of platform capitalism argue that users retain agency: one can always log off. Yet
this argument overlooks asymmetry. When billion-dollar corporations refine persuasive
technologies using troves of behavioural data, the individual’s “choice” becomes less sovereign
than it appears. The imbalance resembles a contest where one side writes the rules while the
other merely participates.
None of this necessitates technological pessimism. Digital innovation has democratized
expression and expanded access to knowledge. But a regulatory imagination that lags behind
technological acceleration risks allowing attention to be mined without accountability. A
society that cannot protect its collective focus may find its democracy subtly diluted — not by
censorship, but by distraction.
Source: The Indian Express, Editorial Section, Title: The Attention Economy and the Cost of
Distraction

Il.	Governments across the world are embracing data as the new grammar of governance.
Dashboards glow with real-time indicators; welfare schemes are monitored through biometric
authentication; predictive analytics promises to anticipate everything from disease outbreaks
to tax evasion. Efficiency, we are told, will no longer be aspirational but algorithmic.
Yet the seduction of quantification carries risks. Data, for all its apparent objectivity, is
neither neutral nor complete. It is collected through institutional lenses, filtered through
technical assumptions, and interpreted within political contexts. What cannot be easily
measured — dignity, exclusion, informal labor, social trust — often recedes from policy
imagination. When governance becomes synonymous with metrics, what is immeasurable risks
becoming invisible.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Proponents argue that digitization reduces corruption and leakages. There is merit in that
claim. However, technological centralization can also concentrate power. When databases
converge and identifiers become mandatory, the citizen’s autonomy may shrink even as
administrative efficiency expands. The architecture of surveillance is rarely built overnight; it
accumulates incrementally, justified at each step by convenience.
None of this is an argument against data itself. Evidence-based policymaking is indispensable
in complex societies. But democratic oversight must evolve as rapidly as technological capacity.
Without transparency, accountability, and meaningful consent, data-driven governance may
promise precision while delivering opacity. The challenge is not to abandon metrics, but to
embed them within constitutional ethics.
Source: The Hindu, Editorial Section, Title: The Perils of Data-Driven Governance

platforms, commitments are articulated with solemn urgency; domestically, however,
environmental safeguards are frequently diluted in the name of expediency. The result is a
climate politics that appears ambitious in rhetoric but ambivalent in execution.

camps. Climate change is not merely an environmental issue; it is an equity issue disguised as
weather.

pragmatism curdles into complacency. The language of balance — growth versus green, jobs

XI.	Section 504 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) proscribes intentional insult with intent to
provoke breach of public peace. In Fiona Shrikhande v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme
Court delineated three essential ingredients constituting the offence under Section 504 IPC:
(a) intentional insult; (b) the insult must be of such nature as to give provocation to the person
insulted; and (c) the accused must intend or know that such provocation would cause another
to break the public peace or commit any other offence. The intentional insult must be of
sufficient degree to provoke a person to break public peace or commit another offence. Mere
abusive language, absent the requisite provocative element and mental state, does not ipso
facto satisfy Section 504. Significantly, the Supreme Court clarified that verbatim reproduction
of offending words in the complaint is not mandated. Rather, the Magistrate must read the
complaint holistically and determine prima facie whether intentional insult coupled with
provocative potential exists. Background facts, circumstances, the occasion, the manner of
utterance, the addressee, temporal context, and the accused's conduct constitute relevant
considerations in evaluating complaints under Section 504 IPC. As articulated in B.V. Ram
Kumar v. State of Telangana, if the Magistrate, upon reading the complaint as a whole,
concludes prima facie that an intentional insult was made with capacity to provoke breach of
public peace or commission of another offence, the complaint falls within Section 504's ambit.
Critically, Section 504 operates as an inchoate offence—it does not require proof that public
peace was actually broken or that another offence was in fact committed. The statutory focus
rests on the tendency and likelihood of provocation leading to such consequences, not
accomplished disturbance. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) provides procedural
mechanisms governing private complaints alleging offences like Section 504. Section 200 CrPC
mandates examination of the complainant and witnesses on oath, forming the foundational
step in complaint cases. Section 202 CrPC permits postponement of process issuance where the
Magistrate considers it necessary to conduct a preliminary inquiry or investigation to verify
whether sufficient grounds exist to proceed. This provision operates as an optional safeguard
against mechanical process issuance. Where complaints fail to disclose essential ingredients or
constitute abuse of process, the High Court may exercise inherent jurisdiction under Section
482 CrPC to quash proceedings. This power ensures prevention of unjust continuation of
proceedings and secures justice, distinguishing it from appellate re-appreciation under Section
3897 CrPC or compounding under Section 320 CrPC. Section 504 IPC must be distinguished
from Section 506 IPC (criminal intimidation), which addresses threats intended to cause alarm
or compel action or inaction, rather than provocative insults aimed at breaching public peace.
The two provisions protect distinct legal interests and operate on different factual matrices.

XII. Abetment is a foundational concept in criminal law that deals with the culpability of
individuals who, although may not commit the actual offence themselves, play a vital role in
facilitating or provoking its commission. Section 107 defines abetment in three distinct forms.
First, a person abets an offence if he instigates another person to do that act. Instigation
means actively suggesting, encouraging, or provoking someone to commit an offence. Mere
words can amount to instigation if they are intended to incite. Secondly, abetment also occurs
when a person engages in a conspiracy with others for committing an offence, and some act or
illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy. Mere agreement is not enough
unless followed by some act. Thirdly, a person abets by intentionally aiding the doing of an
offence. This includes providing tools, information, or facilitating the offence in any manner.
